synopsis: The booklet concludes that compute is cheap relative to engineering labor, but its value depends on simulated time delivered per wall-clock hour; real-time factors must be benchmarked on the actual machine geometry and sensor set [f198, f8309, f13424, f13425]. Recorded-data replay, semantic/object-list replay and SIL are economical routes to large test volumes, whereas coupled high-fidelity terrain models are unsuitable for exhaustive sweeps and excessive fidelity threatens the four-month validation window [f332, f5257, f527, f6103, f13063]. Sensor and weather compute costs span more than three orders of magnitude: examples include 14 hours for a 12-second CPU radar scenario, approximately 12 ms per GPU radar frame, and 20 seconds per diffusion-weather image, but these are examples rather than planning constants [f4451, f4453, f4454, f4456, f12963]. Listed GPU rates are about USD 1.734–1.861 per hour; the booklet estimates ten continuously running GPUs over four months at roughly USD 54,000 and at most about 29,000 GPU-hours, limiting full-sensor-fidelity scenario coverage [f8310, f8311, f8312, f8313]. The assumed thousands of nightly runs and throughput for about 6,000 zero-miss trials across 20 strata plus hundreds of exposure hours remain unquantified, with a recommendation to fix the run and physical-correlation budget before mid-2027 [f7450, f7449, f7451]. Actual program compute, capacity and triage costs are absent from the brief, independent published off-road safety-validation compute costs and ROI were not found, and the proposed compute/triage bottleneck lacks program-specific evidence [f10739, f10615, f10789, f10790].
